title: Course syllabus: 3MB001
text:
Summary of the official syllabus. The syllabus itself is the binding version: https://www.umu.se/en/education/syllabus/3mb001/ (Swedish: https://www.umu.se/utbildning/kurs-och-utbildningsplan/3mb001/)



English title: Cell Biology
Swedish title: Cellbiologi
Course code: 3MB001 (replaces the earlier 3MB038 Cellbiologi)
Credits: 15 ECTS
Education level: First cycle
Main fields of study: Molecular Biology; Biomedical Sciences (both first cycle, less than 60 credits of first-cycle courses as entry requirements)
Grading scale: Three-grade scale (U / G / VG)
Responsible department: Department of Molecular Biology
Established: by PRBMT, 2025-10-27
Validity: 2027-01-18 and until further notice
First run: spring 2027, 18 January to 24 March 2027, on campus in Umeå, taught in English





Theory. Fundamental theory in modern molecular cell biology. This site covers this module.
PPT: Working Life and Career. Oral presentations, seminar discussions, problem solving, a poster on a biomedical problem for a commissioning party, and projects as a working method.
Laboratory Work. Cell biology methods: planning and running experiments, analysing and presenting data, writing results in scientific form.




Knowledge and Understanding. The student should be able to:

Describe the structure and function of the cell and explain methods used to study cell biological processes.
Explain the structure and function of cell membranes and the principles of membrane transport.
Describe fundamental principles of cell communication and signal transduction.
Describe how proteins are handled and regulated in the cell.
Compare the structure and function of different organelles and explain their roles in cellular homeostasis.
Explain the basis of cell shape, motility, and intracellular transport, and give examples of methods used to study these processes.
Describe the regulation of the cell cycle and the mechanisms of cell division.
Describe different forms of programmed cell death and their regulation.
Explain basic concepts of cell biological disease mechanisms.

Skills and Abilities. The student should be able to:

Present scientific content orally in a clear and structured manner.
Collaborate in groups to solve cell biological problems and communicate the results effectively.
Participate in structured scientific discussions and critically reflect on theoretical and practical content.
Plan and conduct basic experiments in cell biology.
Apply good laboratory practice and follow established protocols.
Analyze and present experimental data in written form.
Interpret results and draw conclusions based on scientific principles.
Demonstrate skills and the ability to identify, formulate, and propose solutions to a problem relevant to the education, based on labor market needs
Demonstrate the ability to define and describe projects as a working method.

Judgement and Approach. The student should be able to:

Identify one’s own learning needs and take responsibility for further learning




20 ECTS in chemistry, of which at least 5 ECTS in biochemistry (or 20 ECTS in chemistry combined with physics and/or mathematics, of which at least 5 ECTS in biochemistry); 20 ECTS in biology, including microbiology, molecular biology and genetics.



Lectures plus student-centred teaching: interactive seminars, case-based learning and practical work. All teaching except lectures is mandatory. Lab work requires knowing the lab safety rules and basic GLP. Taught in English (Swedish if no participant needs English).

title: Study questions: seeing cells (microscopy)
text:
G-level questions
1. Explain the difference between magnification and resolution. Why can a light microscope not separate two objects that are 50 nm apart, however much it magnifies? [ELO 1]






Model answer





Magnification is how much bigger the image is than the object. Resolution is the smallest distance at which two points can still be seen as two. Light is a wave, so a lens turns each point of the sample into a small blur spot. When two points are closer than about \(0.61\,\lambda/\mathrm{NA}\), their blur spots merge into one. With visible light (about 500 nm) and the best objectives (NA about 1.4) this limit is about 200 nm. Two objects 50 nm apart give one blob, and magnifying the blob more adds no detail.




2. Describe how a phase-contrast microscope and a DIC microscope make living, unstained cells visible. Why is staining with dyes usually not an option for living cells? [ELO 1]






Model answer





Unstained cells absorb almost no light, but dense structures (nucleus, membranes) have a higher refractive index and slow light down (phase shift). Phase contrast converts these phase shifts into differences in brightness. DIC uses polarised light to turn gradients in optical path into light and shadow, so edges look three-dimensional. Most dyes for bright-field microscopy need the cells to be fixed and often sectioned, and many dyes are toxic, so stained cells are dead.




3. Draw and label the light path in an epifluorescence microscope with a filter cube for a green fluorophore. State what each filter and the dichroic mirror does. [ELO 1]






Model answer





Lamp → excitation filter (passes only blue light that excites the fluorophore) → dichroic mirror (reflects blue light down through the objective onto the sample) → fluorophore absorbs blue and emits green → green light goes back up through the objective → passes through the dichroic mirror (it transmits longer wavelengths) → emission filter (passes green, blocks stray blue) → camera or eye. The design works because of the Stokes shift: emitted light has a longer wavelength than the excitation light.




4. Describe the steps of indirect immunofluorescence to show where tubulin is in cultured cells. Why do we use a secondary antibody? [ELO 1] [ELO 6]






Model answer






Fix the cells (e.g. formaldehyde) so proteins are cross-linked and stay in place. 2. Permeabilise the membranes with a mild detergent so antibodies can enter. 3. Block free binding sites (e.g. with serum proteins) to reduce background. 4. Add the primary antibody against tubulin (e.g. made in mouse), wash. 5. Add a fluorescent secondary antibody against mouse antibodies, wash. 6. Often add a DNA dye (DAPI), mount and image. The secondary antibody amplifies the signal (several secondaries bind each primary), and one labelled secondary can be used with many different primaries from the same species.





5. What is GFP, why was it so useful for cell biology, and how is a GFP fusion protein made? [ELO 1] [ELO 6]






Model answer





GFP is the green fluorescent protein from the jellyfish Aequorea victoria. Its chain of 238 amino acids folds into a barrel and forms its fluorescent group by itself (it needs only oxygen), so the gene works in any cell. To make a fusion protein you join the coding sequence of the protein of interest to the GFP coding sequence in the same reading frame, without a stop codon between them, and introduce the DNA into cells. The cell makes one chain, protein–GFP, so you can see where the protein is in a living cell and follow it over time. Mutants of GFP and proteins from corals give other colours, so several proteins can be followed at once.




6. Explain how a confocal microscope gives sharper images of thick samples than a wide-field fluorescence microscope. What is the cost? [ELO 1]






Model answer





In wide-field fluorescence the whole depth of the sample is lit, so out-of-focus light adds haze. A confocal microscope focuses a laser spot in the sample and places a pinhole in front of the detector at the point where light from the focal plane is focused. Light from other depths is out of focus at the pinhole and mostly blocked. The spot is scanned to build the image. This gives a thin optical section (about 0.5–1 µm), and a stack of sections gives a 3D image. Costs: it is slower (point by point), and the sample receives more light, so there is more photobleaching and phototoxicity.




7. Name two problems you meet when you film living fluorescent cells for many hours, and one way to reduce each. [ELO 1]






Model answer





Photobleaching: fluorophores are destroyed by repeated excitation, so the signal fades. Phototoxicity: excited fluorophores make reactive oxygen species that damage the cell, so it may behave abnormally or die. Both are reduced by using less light (lower intensity, shorter exposures, fewer time points, a more sensitive camera) and gentler methods such as spinning-disk confocal or light-sheet microscopy, which light less of the sample. The cells must also be kept at 37 °C with the right CO₂ and medium.




8. Compare TEM and SEM: how is the image made, what does each show, and why can neither be used on living cells? [ELO 1]






Model answer





TEM: electrons pass through an ultrathin section (about 50–100 nm) stained with heavy metals; areas that scatter electrons look dark. It shows internal structure (membranes, organelles, ribosomes) at about 1–2 nm. SEM: a fine beam scans a metal-coated sample, and electrons knocked out of the surface are detected. It shows the 3D surface at a few nm. Both work in a vacuum, so samples are fixed and dried (and for TEM embedded and cut), which kills the cells.




9. What is single-particle cryo-EM? Explain why averaging many images is needed and what the result is. [ELO 1]






Model answer





A purified protein or complex is frozen so quickly that water forms glass-like ice, keeping the molecules in their native, hydrated shape without stain. Only a low electron dose can be used, so each image of a single molecule is very noisy. A computer finds tens of thousands to millions of particle images, sorts them by viewing angle and averages them, so noise cancels and the signal remains. The 2D views are combined into a 3D density map, often at better than 0.3 nm, into which an atomic model is built.

title: Study questions: seeing cells (microscopy)
text:
VG-style questions
10. [VG] A research group makes a GFP fusion of a newly discovered protein, P. In living cells, P–GFP is spread evenly through the cytosol. But immunofluorescence with an antibody against P in fixed cells shows P on mitochondria. Give two possible explanations, and propose an experiment to decide between them. [ELO 1]






Model answer





Possible explanations:

The GFP tag disturbs targeting. If P has a mitochondrial targeting signal at its N-terminus and GFP was fused there, the signal may be hidden; or the fusion is overexpressed so much that the import machinery is saturated and the excess stays in the cytosol.
The antibody is not specific. It may bind another, mitochondrial protein, so the immunofluorescence result is wrong.
(Also acceptable) Fixation artefact: soluble proteins can be extracted or moved during fixation and permeabilisation.

Experiments: put GFP at the other end of P and express it at low level (e.g. from the gene’s own promoter, or by tagging the endogenous gene with CRISPR); check if it then goes to mitochondria (co-stain with a mitochondrial marker). Test the antibody on cells lacking P (knockout or knockdown): if mitochondria are still stained, the antibody is not specific. Biochemistry can add independent evidence: fractionate cells and test which fraction contains P on a western blot (next lecture).




11. [VG] You want to know (a) how often vesicles carrying a GFP-tagged cargo move along microtubules in living cells, and (b) whether the cargo sits inside the vesicle or on its outer membrane. Design an imaging approach for each part, and explain why one method cannot answer both. [ELO 1] [ELO 6]






Model answer






Live-cell fluorescence imaging of the GFP-cargo, ideally with microtubules labelled in a second colour (e.g. a red fluorescent tubulin fusion), using a fast, gentle method (spinning-disk confocal or light-sheet) and short exposures to limit bleaching and phototoxicity. Track vesicles over time and count runs along microtubules. Control: a drug that depolymerises microtubules should stop the directed runs.
A vesicle is about 50–100 nm across, below the 200 nm light limit, so inside versus outside cannot be decided with ordinary light microscopy. Use immuno-electron microscopy: fix cells, label the cargo (anti-GFP antibody with gold particles) on thin sections, and see whether the gold is in the lumen or on the cytosolic face of the vesicle membrane. Cryo-electron tomography or super-resolution would also help.

One method cannot do both because live imaging needs light microscopy (low resolution, living cells), while the nanometre question needs EM (high resolution, but dead or frozen cells). Combining them on the same cells is called correlative light and electron microscopy (CLEM).




12. [VG] Explain why the SARS-CoV-2 spike in the mRNA COVID-19 vaccines carries two extra prolines (the “2P” spike), and why cryo-EM was a good method to check this design quickly. [ELO 1]






Model answer





The spike is a fusion protein: it starts in a compact prefusion shape and, when it fuses the viral and cell membranes, S1 is lost and S2 refolds into a long postfusion rod. Many protective (neutralising) antibodies recognise the prefusion shape, but a spike made on its own can flip to the postfusion form. Two prolines, which are stiff, placed at a hinge in S2 block this refolding and keep the prefusion shape, so the immune system sees the right target. The idea came from structures of related coronavirus spikes (MERS, SARS). Cryo-EM was ideal because the spike is a large, flexible, glycosylated membrane-protein trimer that is hard to crystallise; cryo-EM needs only a small amount of purified protein, no crystals, and keeps it in a near-native state. In early 2020 a cryo-EM structure confirmed within weeks that the SARS-CoV-2 2P spike holds the prefusion shape.

title: Quiz: a tour of the cell
text:
Short questions to check that you can use the map of the cell from the lecture. Try each on paper first, then open the hint, and only then the answer.

Q1. [ELO 1] Name three structures that a eukaryotic animal cell has and a bacterium does not.






Hint





Think of everything that is surrounded by its own membrane inside the cell.









Answer





Any three of: a nucleus with a double membrane (nuclear envelope), endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, endosomes and lysosomes, mitochondria, peroxisomes, and a cytoskeleton with microtubules organised by a centrosome. A bacterium has a plasma membrane, ribosomes and DNA in a nucleoid, but almost no internal membranes.




Q2. [ELO 1] Which of these spaces are on the same side of a membrane as the outside of the cell: cytosol, ER lumen, nucleoplasm, lysosome lumen, Golgi lumen?






Hint





Which compartments exchange material with the outside by vesicles that bud and fuse? Which are joined by open pores?









Answer





The ER lumen, the Golgi lumen and the lysosome lumen are topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell: vesicles carry material between them and the outside without crossing a membrane. The cytosol and the nucleoplasm form the other side; they are joined through nuclear pores.




Q3. [ELO 1] Put these in order from smallest to largest, and give a typical size for each: ribosome, mitochondrion (width), protein, nucleus, potassium ion, virus such as influenza.






Hint





Each step on the scale ladder was roughly a factor of 3–10.









Answer





Potassium ion (~0.3 nm) < protein (~5 nm) < ribosome (~25 nm) < influenza virus (~100 nm) < mitochondrion (~1 µm wide) < nucleus (~5–10 µm).




Q4. [ELO 1] A protein diffuses across a 10 µm cell in a few seconds. About how long would it take to diffuse 100 µm? What does this tell you about very long cells such as nerve cells?






Hint





Diffusion time grows with the square of the distance: \(t \approx x^2 / 6D\).









Answer





Ten times the distance means \(10^2 = 100\) times the time: a few hundred seconds, that is several minutes. Over a metre, the time becomes hundreds of years. So long cells such as nerve cells cannot rely on diffusion; they carry cargo with motor proteins along the cytoskeleton.




Q5. [ELO 5] A cell type is packed with rough ER and Golgi. What does the cell probably spend most of its effort on? Give one example of such a cell.






Hint





What does the rough ER make, and where do those proteins go?









Answer





It probably secretes large amounts of protein. The rough ER makes proteins for secretion and the Golgi modifies and sorts them. Examples: a pancreatic acinar cell (digestive enzymes) or a plasma cell (antibodies).




Q6. [ELO 1] A membrane receptor has a sugar chain on one domain. On which side of the plasma membrane do you expect to find that domain, and why?






Hint





Sugar chains are added in the lumen of the ER and Golgi. Follow the protein from the ER to the plasma membrane.









Answer





On the outside of the cell. The sugar chain is added while that domain faces the ER and Golgi lumen. Vesicles bud and fuse without the protein flipping, so the lumen-facing side ends up facing the outside of the cell.




Q7. [ELO 1] Give one advantage and one limitation of using HeLa cells to study a human protein.






Hint





Think of what a cell line is, and where HeLa came from.









Answer





Advantage: human cells that divide without limit, are cheap and easy to grow, image and perturb, and are used in many labs, so results can be compared. Limitation: HeLa cells are cancer cells with an abnormal genome (about 80 chromosomes) and an HPV infection that disables normal cell-cycle brakes; they grow flat on plastic, so they may not behave like a normal cell in a tissue. (Also acceptable: contamination of other cell lines, or the ethical questions about consent.)




Q8. [ELO 1] Electron microscopy of thin sections first showed the ER and ribosomes. Why was another method also needed to understand what lysosomes do?






Hint





What does a picture tell you, and what does it not tell you?









Answer





A micrograph shows where a structure is and what it looks like, but not what it does. Cell fractionation (breaking cells and separating their parts by centrifugation, then measuring enzyme activities in each fraction) showed that one fraction held digestive enzymes that work at acidic pH: the lysosomes.

About this lecture
This is the first lecture of the course. It gives you a map of the cell that every later lecture uses.
After this lecture you can:

Name the main compartments of an animal cell and say in one sentence what each one does.
Explain topology: which spaces are on the cytosol side of a membrane and which are on the lumen side.
Give the size and number of the things inside a cell (ions, proteins, ribosomes, organelles, cells) to within a factor of ten.
Choose a model system (yeast, a cell line such as HeLa, an organoid) for a question, and say what it cannot tell you.

ELO 1 (parts of the cell, methods) and ELO 5 (organelles compared; this lecture is the first look).

Welcome to Cell Biology. This first lecture is a guided tour. We will not go deep into any one organelle today; every organelle you see here gets its own lecture later. The aim is a mental map that you can hang the rest of the course on. Keep three ideas in mind. First, the cell is divided into compartments by membranes, and the chemistry inside each compartment is different. Second, every membrane has two sides, and knowing which side is which, the topology, explains a lot of later material on protein sorting and vesicle traffic. Third, sizes and numbers matter: a protein is about five nanometres, a cell is about fifteen micrometres, and a cell holds billions of protein molecules. At the end we look at how we study cells, using model systems, and at HeLa cells: the most used human cells in research, and a story about consent that every biomedical scientist should know. This lecture belongs to ELO 1 and is the first step towards ELO 5.

The course map: from molecules to cells

You already think in molecules: DNA, proteins, enzymes, ΔG. This course moves you one level up: to compartments (where things are), machines (what moves and signals) and decisions (divide, move or die), and to disease when these go wrong.

Here is the whole course on one slide. On the left is what you bring from biochemistry, molecular biology and chemistry: molecules, reactions, equilibria and the central dogma. We will not teach these again. The course moves you up one level of organisation. The first blocks are about compartments: what a cell is made of and how we study it, then membranes and transport, then how proteins are made, folded and sent to the right organelle. The middle blocks are about signals and machines: how a cell senses its surroundings and how the cytoskeleton gives it shape and movement. Then come decisions: when to divide and when to die. The last block is disease, seen as cell biology going wrong. Each block is one or more expected learning outcomes, ELOs, and the ELO numbers on the tiles are the same numbers as on the exam. Every lecture also ends with a drug or a disease, so you see why the mechanism matters for medicine and drug development.

title: A tour of the cell
section: The question: how does one small drop do everything at once?
text:
The question: how does one small drop do everything at once?


A cultured animal cell holds about 2 picolitres of water, and in it:

billions of protein molecules, many thousands of different kinds,
enzymes that make fats next to enzymes that burn them,
enzymes that digest proteins at pH 5, in a cell whose cytosol is pH 7.2,
DNA that must be copied once per division and never digested.

How does the cell keep incompatible chemistry apart, and still get every molecule to the place where it is needed?






Cultured endothelial cells. Blue: nucleus (DNA). Green: microtubules. Red: actin filaments.


Look at the image. These are cultured cells from a cow blood vessel, stained with three fluorescent dyes: blue for DNA in the nucleus, green for microtubules and red for actin filaments. Even with only three stains you can see order: the nucleus sits in the middle, microtubules spread out from near the nucleus, and actin lines the cell edge. Now the puzzle. Each cell is a tiny volume, about two picolitres, but inside it there are billions of protein molecules doing thousands of reactions at once. Some of these reactions would destroy each other if they were mixed. Digestive enzymes that work best at pH 5 would attack the cell’s own proteins. Fat synthesis and fat breakdown would cancel each other out. DNA must be kept safe and copied exactly once per cycle. The answer, which the rest of this lecture develops, has three parts: compartments separated by membranes, transport routes between the compartments, and a cytoskeleton that organises space. Keep this question in mind; we come back to it in the summary.

This is a recap of what you met in microbiology. A bacterium such as E. coli is about two micrometres long. It has a plasma membrane, usually a cell wall, ribosomes and its DNA in a region called the nucleoid, but no membrane around the DNA and almost no internal membranes. A eukaryotic cell is about a thousand times larger in volume. That is the key point on this slide: a bigger cell has a problem. Its surface is small compared with its volume, and molecules must travel further. Eukaryotes solve this with internal membranes, which add a large membrane area for reactions and divide the volume into compartments with different chemistry. Notice the mitochondria on the right: they are about the size of a bacterium. That is not a coincidence. Mitochondria come from a bacterium that was taken up by an ancestral cell, and they still have their own DNA and ribosomes. We come back to this in the mitochondria lecture.

title: A tour of the cell
section: A map of the animal cell
text:
A map of the animal cell


This is the map we use in the whole course, and the colours are fixed: every later lecture uses the same colour for the same organelle. Purple is the nucleus, teal the endoplasmic reticulum, orange the Golgi apparatus, red the mitochondria, green the endosomes and lysosomes, blue the peroxisomes, grey the cytoskeleton, and brown the plasma membrane. Start in the centre. The nucleus holds the DNA, surrounded by the nuclear envelope, which is two membranes with pores through them. The outer nuclear membrane continues into the endoplasmic reticulum, the ER. The rough ER has ribosomes on its surface and makes membrane proteins and proteins for secretion; the smooth ER makes lipids and stores calcium. Proteins go from the ER to the Golgi, which modifies and sorts them, and then on to the plasma membrane in secretory vesicles, or to lysosomes. Material taken in from outside goes to endosomes and then to lysosomes for digestion. Mitochondria make most of the ATP. The centrosome organises the microtubules. Everything else, the fluid between the organelles, is the cytosol. The picture is a simplification: a real cell has hundreds of mitochondria and a much larger ER.

This table is the text version of the map. Do not learn the percentages by heart; learn the pattern. About half of a typical cell is cytosol, and the cytosol is where proteins are made on free ribosomes and where much of metabolism happens, for example glycolysis. Each membrane-bound organelle has a special job, and each has its own lecture, shown in the right column. Notice that the amounts depend on what the cell does. A liver cell, which does a lot of metabolism, has many mitochondria, about a fifth of its volume. A pancreatic acinar cell, which secretes large amounts of digestive enzymes, is packed with rough ER. A plasma cell, which secretes antibodies, also has a lot of rough ER. So you can often guess what a cell does by looking at its organelles under an electron microscope, and the reverse is also true. Two jobs are worth noting now because they come back: mitochondria do not only make ATP, they also start one form of cell death; and the ER is the main calcium store of the cell, which matters for signalling.

title: A tour of the cell
section: Two sides of every membrane: topology
text:
Two sides of every membrane: topology


This is the most important idea of today, because it explains much of protein sorting and vesicle traffic later. Every membrane separates two spaces. Look at the colours. The light yellow space is the cytosol side: the cytosol itself and the inside of the nucleus, the nucleoplasm. These two are joined through nuclear pores, which are large open channels, so they count as one space. The light blue space is the lumen side: the inside of the ER, the gap between the two nuclear membranes, the Golgi, the vesicles, endosomes and lysosomes. The lumen side is, in topology, the same as the outside of the cell. Why? Because these compartments are connected to the outside by vesicles that bud from one membrane and fuse with another, without a molecule ever crossing a membrane. A protein secreted from the ER lumen reaches the outside without ever being in the cytosol. Mitochondria are the exception: their inner space, the matrix, is a third space of its own, a legacy of their bacterial origin. Peroxisomes, not shown here, also import their proteins from the cytosol.

title: A tour of the cell
section: Inside-out logic: a protein keeps its orientation
text:
Inside-out logic: a protein keeps its orientation


The part of a protein that is in the ER lumen ends up outside the cell.
This is why sugar chains (added in the ER and Golgi lumen) are found on the outer surface of the cell, and why receptors have their binding site outside.


Here is topology in action. A membrane protein is made in the ER membrane. One part of it faces the ER lumen, and in the lumen the cell adds sugar chains to it. The other part, the tail, faces the cytosol. Now follow it. A vesicle buds from the ER: the lumen side of the protein now faces the inside of the vesicle. The vesicle fuses with the Golgi: the lumen side faces the Golgi lumen. A new vesicle carries it to the plasma membrane and fuses: now the lumen side faces the outside of the cell. At no step does the protein flip, and at no step does any part of it cross a membrane. So the rule is simple: lumen side equals outside. This explains why all the sugar chains of the cell surface face outwards, and why a hormone receptor made in the ER has its hormone-binding part outside the cell and its signalling part in the cytosol. When we study receptors and protein sorting, you will use this rule again and again. It is also a common exam question.

title: A tour of the cell
section: The scale ladder: from ion to cell
text:
The scale ladder: from ion to cell

Each step on the axis is a factor of 10. A cell is about 50,000× wider than an ion and about 3000× wider than a protein.

Cell biology covers about five orders of magnitude in size, so the axis is logarithmic: each tick is ten times the one before. An ion such as potassium is about a third of a nanometre across. A typical protein is about five nanometres. A ribosome, a large machine made of RNA and about eighty proteins, is about twenty-five nanometres. Many viruses, such as influenza or SARS coronavirus 2, are about a hundred nanometres. A bacterium and a mitochondrion are about one micrometre wide. The nucleus is a few micrometres, and a whole animal cell is ten to twenty micrometres. The bars at the bottom link to the next lecture. A light microscope cannot separate two objects closer than about two hundred nanometres, so with light you can see cells, nuclei and mitochondria, but not single ribosomes or proteins, unless you label them with a fluorescent tag. An electron microscope sees down to about a nanometre in a thin section of a cell. Remember these sizes: they let you check whether an answer is reasonable.

Rough values of the kind collected in BioNumbers (bionumbers.hms.harvard.edu) and Cell Biology by the Numbers (Milo and Phillips). Diffusion time: t \approx x^2 / 6D with D \approx 5–10\ \mu\text{m}^2/\text{s} for a protein in cytoplasm.

These are numbers to remember as orders of magnitude, not exact values. A cell holds about one to ten billion protein molecules. Spread over a volume of a few picolitres, that is a protein concentration of a few hundred milligrams per millilitre: the cytoplasm is crowded, more like a gel than like water. Now diffusion. For a molecule that moves randomly, the time to travel a distance x grows with x squared: t is roughly x squared divided by six times the diffusion coefficient. A protein in cytoplasm has a diffusion coefficient of about five to ten square micrometres per second, so it crosses a ten-micrometre cell in a few seconds. That is fast enough for most signals. But because of the x squared, diffusion becomes useless over long distances: to diffuse one metre, from your spinal cord to your foot along a nerve axon, would take hundreds of years. This is why cells have motor proteins that carry cargo along the cytoskeleton, which you meet in the cytoskeleton block. Small molecules such as glucose diffuse about ten to a hundred times faster than proteins.

title: A tour of the cell
section: How do we know? Electron microscopy revealed the compartments
text:
How do we know? Electron microscopy revealed the compartments



Light microscopy (from the 1600s) showed cells and nuclei, but nothing smaller than ~0.2 µm.
1940s–1950s: the electron microscope and thin sections showed the ER, ribosomes, Golgi stacks and the inner structure of mitochondria.
At the same time, cell fractionation (breaking cells and separating parts by centrifugation) showed what each part does, for example lysosomes full of digestive enzymes.
Nobel Prize 1974: Claude, de Duve and Palade.

Lesson: one method shows where; another shows what it does. You need both.






Transmission electron micrograph of a human B lymphocyte. Large nucleus with dark chromatin; mitochondria with folded inner membranes in the cytoplasm. Scale bar 500 nm.


How do we know that the map is true? Until the 1940s, the light microscope was the main tool, and it cannot resolve anything smaller than about two hundred nanometres. Cells and nuclei were visible, and mitochondria as tiny dots, but the ER and ribosomes were invisible. The electron microscope uses electrons instead of light, and electrons have a much shorter wavelength, so it resolves structures down to about a nanometre. When researchers learned to cut cells into very thin sections, they suddenly saw the membranes inside cells: the ER, ribosomes, the Golgi stacks and the folded inner membrane of mitochondria. In the image you see a human B lymphocyte: the large nucleus with dark, condensed chromatin, and mitochondria with their folded inner membrane. But a picture shows where things are, not what they do. At the same time, others broke cells open and separated their parts by centrifugation, then measured enzymes in each fraction. This is how lysosomes and peroxisomes were discovered. Combining the two methods won the Nobel Prize in 1974. Microscopy and fractionation are the topics of the next two lectures.

text:

Yeast genetics found the genes for the cell cycle (Nobel 2001), vesicle traffic (2013) and autophagy (2016).






Budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae (DIC microscopy). Small buds are daughter cells growing out of the mother cells.


No single system answers every question, so cell biologists choose a model system. The rule is to use the simplest system that still has the feature you want to study. Bacteria are fast and simple but have no organelles. Budding yeast, the yeast used for baking and brewing, is the simplest common eukaryote: it has a nucleus, ER, Golgi and mitochondria, it divides in about ninety minutes, and its genes are easy to delete. Because most of the core machinery is shared with human cells, yeast genetics found the genes that control the cell cycle, the genes for vesicle traffic and the genes for autophagy, and each of these won a Nobel Prize. In the image you see yeast cells with buds; each bud is a new daughter cell. Human cell lines give human proteins in a dish. Organoids add three-dimensional tissue structure. Mice give a whole body. Each step up is closer to a patient but slower, more expensive and harder to control. In a VG question you may be asked to choose a system and to say what it cannot show.

title: A tour of the cell
section: Cell lines: HeLa, the first human cells that never stopped dividing
text:
Cell lines: HeLa, the first human cells that never stopped dividing



Normal human cells divide only about 40–60 times in culture, then stop.
A cell line divides without limit. Most come from tumours.
HeLa (1951) came from the cervical tumour of Henrietta Lacks. It was the first human cell line.
HeLa cells carry human papillomavirus 18 (HPV-18). Viral proteins switch off two brakes on cell division (you meet them in the cell-cycle and cancer lectures).
HeLa is not a normal cell: about 80 chromosomes instead of 46. And HeLa grows so well that it has contaminated many other cell lines, so labs now check the identity of their cells with a DNA test.







Living HeLa cells. Blue: nucleus. Green: microtubules. Red: mitochondria. Scale bar 10 µm.


Most cells taken from a human body divide a limited number of times in a dish, about forty to sixty times, and then stop. A cell line is a population of cells that can divide without limit. Almost all human cell lines come from tumours, because cancer cells have lost the normal limits on division. The first human cell line came from Henrietta Lacks, a thirty-one-year-old African American woman treated for cervical cancer at Johns Hopkins Hospital in Baltimore in 1951. Her cells, named HeLa from her name, grew faster than any human cells before them. We now know why. Her tumour was caused by human papillomavirus type 18, and viral proteins in HeLa cells switch off two key brakes on cell division, proteins called p53 and Rb, which you meet in the cell-cycle and cancer lectures. HeLa cells also have an abnormal genome, with about eighty chromosomes. In the image you see living HeLa cells with three fluorescent labels: nucleus, microtubules and mitochondria. Note the scale bar: these cells are about twenty to forty micrometres long when they spread on glass.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
text:
Organoids: tissue in a dish



An organoid is a small 3D structure that grows from stem cells in a gel, with the right growth factors.
The cells organise themselves: an intestinal organoid forms crypts and a lumen, with several cell types, like the real gut lining.
Organoids can be grown from one patient’s biopsy, so you can test drugs on that patient’s own cells.
Example: in cystic fibrosis, a patient’s intestinal organoids swell when a drug restores the faulty chloride channel (CFTR). The test helps choose a drug for that patient.







Intestinal organoid grown from Lgr5⁺ stem cells. The buds are crypt-like domains around a central lumen.


Cell lines grow as a flat layer on plastic, which is far from a real tissue. Organoids are a newer model, developed from about 2009. You take adult stem cells, for example from the base of an intestinal crypt, put them in a gel that mimics the material around cells in a tissue, and add the growth factors that the stem cells normally receive. The stem cells divide and organise themselves into a small three-dimensional structure with a central lumen and buds that look like crypts, with several cell types, much like the lining of the gut. The image shows such an intestinal organoid. Because organoids can be grown from a small biopsy, they can be made from one patient. A good example is cystic fibrosis, which is caused by a faulty chloride channel called CFTR. When a drug restores channel function in a patient’s intestinal organoids, chloride and water flow into the lumen and the organoids swell. The amount of swelling helps predict whether the drug will work in that patient. You meet ion channels in lecture six and cystic fibrosis again in the disease lectures.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Why it matters: HeLa cells changed medicine
text:
Why it matters: HeLa cells changed medicine


Polio vaccine: poliovirus grows in HeLa, so HeLa was mass-produced to test the Salk vaccine (1953–55).
HPV and cervical cancer: HPV-18 DNA in HeLa helped show that a virus causes cervical cancer (Nobel 2008), which led to the HPV vaccine.
Drug screening: cell lines like HeLa are the first test for thousands of drug candidates: does the compound kill cells, reach its target, change an organelle?


Here is why HeLa cells matter for medicine, and why we tie them back to the cell-line slide. Because HeLa cells were the first human cells that could be grown in large amounts, they became a tool for everything. In the early 1950s, poliovirus was found to grow in HeLa cells. A laboratory at the Tuskegee Institute mass-produced HeLa cells and sent them across the United States to test whether the Salk polio vaccine produced protective antibodies. In the 1980s, researchers found DNA from human papillomavirus type 18 in HeLa cells and in many other cervical cancers. This helped prove that a virus causes cervical cancer, work that won the Nobel Prize in 2008, and it led to the HPV vaccine that is now given to children, including in Sweden. HeLa cells have been used in more than a hundred thousand research papers. Today, cell lines are the first step of drug development: before any animal or human test, a drug candidate is tested on cells. You meet the later phases in the later programme course on clinical trials and drug development.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
section: Why it matters: consent, then and now
text:
Why it matters: consent, then and now



In 1951 Henrietta Lacks was not asked whether her cells could be used. This was common practice at the time. She died the same year, aged 31.
Her family learned about HeLa decades later. Companies sold HeLa cells; the family received nothing.
2013: the HeLa genome was published without the family’s consent. It also says something about her relatives’ DNA. The US National Institutes of Health then agreed with the family on controlled access, with family members on the committee.
Today, in Sweden: research on human tissue needs ethical approval and, as a rule, informed consent. Samples in biobanks are protected by law.

Ask yourself: who should decide how cells from a patient are used, and who should benefit?






HeLa cells, DNA stained with the blue dye Hoechst 33258.


The science of HeLa cannot be separated from the person. Henrietta Lacks was a mother of five who was treated for cervical cancer in a segregated hospital ward in 1951. A sample of her tumour was taken during treatment and given to a research laboratory without her knowledge. This was common practice then, but that does not make it right, and her family did not learn about the cells for more than twenty years. When the HeLa genome sequence was published in 2013, it again happened without asking the family, even though a genome also reveals information about relatives. After discussions, the US National Institutes of Health agreed with the family that the data should be in controlled access, with family members helping to decide who can use it. In 2021 the World Health Organization honoured Henrietta Lacks, and in 2023 the family reached a settlement with a company that had sold HeLa cells. In Sweden today, research on human tissue needs approval from the Swedish Ethical Review Authority, informed consent is the rule, and biobank samples are protected by law. Treat this as a question for discussion, not a closed story.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: A tour of the cell
text:
Summary

A eukaryotic cell is divided by membranes into compartments, each with its own chemistry and job: nucleus, ER, Golgi, endosomes and lysosomes, mitochondria, peroxisomes, and the cytosol between them.
Every membrane has two sides. The cytosol and nucleoplasm form one side; the lumen of the ER, Golgi, vesicles and lysosomes is topologically outside the cell. Mitochondria have a third space.
Sizes and numbers: protein ~5 nm, ribosome ~25 nm, cell 10–20 µm; 10⁹–10¹⁰ proteins per cell; diffusion is fast over a cell but useless over long distances.
We know this from microscopy (where) and fractionation (what), and we study cells in model systems (yeast, cell lines such as HeLa, organoids), each with its limits.

Read more (optional): Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 7th ed., ch. 1 and ch. 12 (first section).
Image credits

Let us return to the opening question: how does one small drop of cytoplasm do everything at once? The answer is compartments. Membranes divide the cell into spaces with different chemistry, such as the acidic lysosome and the calcium-rich ER, and vesicles carry material between the lumen-side compartments without crossing a membrane. Topology is the rule to remember: the lumen side equals the outside of the cell, and the cytosol side includes the nucleus. Sizes and numbers let you check your reasoning, and the diffusion numbers explain why a large cell needs a cytoskeleton and motors. Finally, every fact on today’s map came from methods: electron microscopy showed where structures are, fractionation showed what they do, and model systems let us test ideas. The next two lectures are about these methods: microscopy, and how to take cells apart and perturb them. If you want to read more, chapter one and the first section of chapter twelve of Molecular Biology of the Cell cover today’s material, but the slides and notes are enough for the exam.

title: Study questions: a tour of the cell
text:
G-level questions
1. [ELO 1] Draw a simple animal cell and label the plasma membrane, nucleus, nuclear envelope, rough ER, Golgi apparatus, a mitochondrion, a lysosome and the cytosol. Give one function for each labelled part.






Model answer






Plasma membrane: barrier between cell and outside; controls what enters and leaves.
Nucleus: stores the DNA; transcription happens here.
Nuclear envelope: two membranes with pores; separates nucleoplasm from cytosol but lets molecules pass through pores. The outer membrane continues into the ER.
Rough ER: has ribosomes on its surface; makes membrane proteins and proteins for secretion.
Golgi apparatus: modifies proteins (adds and trims sugar chains) and sorts them to their destination.
Mitochondrion: makes most of the ATP by oxidative phosphorylation.
Lysosome: digests material at about pH 5.
Cytosol: the fluid between organelles; protein synthesis on free ribosomes and much of metabolism (for example glycolysis).





2. [ELO 1] List three differences between a prokaryotic and a eukaryotic cell. Why is it an advantage for a large cell to have internal membranes?






Model answer





Differences: eukaryotes have a nucleus with a nuclear envelope (prokaryote DNA lies in the cytosol); eukaryotes have membrane-bound organelles (ER, Golgi, mitochondria, lysosomes); eukaryotic cells are about 1000 times larger in volume; eukaryotes have an extensive cytoskeleton with motor proteins. Advantage: internal membranes give more membrane area for membrane-bound reactions, and they divide the cell into compartments with different chemistry (for example acidic lysosomes, calcium-rich ER), so incompatible reactions can run at the same time.




3. [ELO 1] Explain what is meant by the lumen of an organelle. Which compartments are topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell, and why?






Model answer





The lumen is the space inside a membrane-bound organelle, on the opposite side of its membrane from the cytosol. The lumens of the ER, the nuclear envelope (the gap between its two membranes), the Golgi, transport vesicles, endosomes and lysosomes are topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell. Material moves between them, and to and from the outside, by vesicles that bud from one membrane and fuse with another, so it never crosses a membrane and never enters the cytosol.




4. [ELO 1] The nucleoplasm is surrounded by two membranes, yet it is said to be on the same side as the cytosol. Explain.






Model answer





The nuclear envelope has nuclear pores: large channels that join the nucleoplasm and the cytosol. Molecules move between them through the pores without crossing a lipid bilayer. The space between the two nuclear membranes, however, is continuous with the ER lumen and is on the lumen side.




5. [ELO 1] Give typical sizes (order of magnitude) for: a protein, a ribosome, a virus, a bacterium, a nucleus and an animal cell. Which of these can you resolve in a light microscope without special methods?






Model answer





Protein ~5 nm; ribosome ~25 nm; virus ~100 nm; bacterium ~1–2 µm; nucleus ~5–10 µm; animal cell ~10–20 µm. The light microscope resolves objects larger than about 0.2 µm, so the bacterium, nucleus and cell can be resolved (and mitochondria, about 1 µm wide). Proteins, ribosomes and most viruses are too small to resolve; single molecules can only be detected if they carry a fluorescent label.




6. [ELO 1] A mammalian cell contains about \(10^9\)–\(10^{10}\) protein molecules in a volume of a few picolitres. What does this mean for the physical state of the cytoplasm, and how fast does a typical protein move across the cell?






Model answer





The protein concentration is a few hundred mg/mL, so the cytoplasm is crowded: more like a gel than a dilute solution. A typical protein diffuses with \(D \approx 5\)–\(10\ \mu\text{m}^2/\text{s}\) in cytoplasm; with \(t \approx x^2/6D\) it crosses a 10 µm cell in a few seconds.




7. [ELO 5] Compare the mitochondrion and the lysosome: number of membranes, main function, and the chemistry of the inner space.






Model answer





Mitochondrion: two membranes (outer and folded inner membrane); main function ATP production by oxidative phosphorylation (also involved in starting apoptosis); the matrix is a separate space with its own DNA and ribosomes, not part of the lumen side. Lysosome: one membrane; digests proteins, lipids and other material; acidic lumen (pH about 4.5–5) full of digestive enzymes; part of the lumen side (reached by vesicles from endosomes).




8. [ELO 1] What is a cell line? Give two reasons why HeLa cells became so widely used, and two reasons to be careful when interpreting results from them.






Model answer





A cell line is a population of cells that divides without limit in culture; normal cells stop after about 40–60 divisions. HeLa became widely used because it was the first human cell line (1951), it grows fast and robustly, and it can be shipped and shared, for example to test the polio vaccine. Reasons for caution: HeLa cells are cancer cells with an abnormal genome (about 80 chromosomes) and HPV-18 proteins that disable cell-cycle brakes; they grow flat on plastic, not in a tissue; and HeLa has contaminated many other cell lines, so the identity of a cell line must be checked with a DNA test.
crumbs: The cell and how we study it

title: Study questions: a tour of the cell
text:
VG-style questions
9. [ELO 1] [VG] A membrane protein has its N-terminus in the ER lumen and its C-terminus in the cytosol. Predict the orientation of the protein (a) in the membrane of a transport vesicle, (b) in the Golgi membrane and (c) in the plasma membrane. A researcher adds an antibody against the N-terminus to living, intact cells. Will the antibody bind? Explain.






Model answer






In the vesicle, the N-terminus faces the vesicle lumen, the C-terminus the cytosol. (b) In the Golgi, the N-terminus faces the Golgi lumen. (c) In the plasma membrane, the N-terminus faces the outside of the cell. The orientation never changes because vesicles bud and fuse without the protein flipping, and the lumen side is topologically equivalent to the outside. The antibody will bind on living cells, because the N-terminus is exposed on the cell surface and an antibody cannot cross the plasma membrane. An antibody against the C-terminus would not bind to intact cells; it would bind only after the membrane is made permeable (for example with a detergent). This is a standard experiment to determine membrane topology.





10. [ELO 1] [VG] You want to know whether a drug that is toxic to the liver damages mitochondria. You can use HeLa cells, budding yeast or organoids grown from human liver cells. Choose a system, justify your choice, and name one thing your system cannot tell you. Suggest a first experiment.






Model answer





A good answer chooses and justifies, and names a limitation. For example: human liver organoids are the best first choice because they are human, contain liver-like cells that metabolise drugs as the liver does (many liver toxins become toxic only after liver enzymes modify them), and can be grown from several donors. Limitation: no blood supply, immune system or other organs, so they cannot show effects that depend on the whole body (for example inflammation, or drug levels in blood). HeLa cells are easier but are cancer cells that may not metabolise the drug like liver cells and rely less on mitochondria. Yeast is good for finding which genes make cells sensitive, but is not human and has a cell wall that may block the drug. First experiment: treat organoids with a range of drug concentrations and an untreated control, then measure mitochondrial function (for example with a dye whose uptake depends on the mitochondrial membrane potential, viewed by fluorescence microscopy) and cell survival, with replicate cultures.




11. [ELO 1] [VG] In a textbook from 1950, the cytoplasm of a cell is described as “a structureless gel with some granules”. Explain, with reference to sizes and methods, why scientists at that time could not see most of the structures on today’s cell map, and which two methods changed this.






Model answer





The light microscope cannot resolve structures closer than about 0.2 µm. Ribosomes (~25 nm), ER membranes (a bilayer is ~5 nm thick, ER tubes ~50–100 nm across) and the inner structure of mitochondria are below this limit, and unstained membranes give little contrast. So the cytoplasm looked structureless, with mitochondria as small granules. Two methods changed this: electron microscopy of thin sections (resolution down to about a nanometre), which showed the ER, ribosomes, Golgi stacks and cristae; and cell fractionation by centrifugation, which separated the parts and showed what each did (for example lysosomes with digestive enzymes). Combining the two gave the modern map.

title: Glossary
text: Key terms used in the course. Definitions are short; follow the link for the full explanation. Add terms here as lectures are written.

title: Glossary
section: The cell and how we study it
text:
The cell and how we study it

A tour of the cell
See A tour of the cell.
Cytosol: the fluid part of the cell between the organelles, where free ribosomes make proteins and much of metabolism takes place.
Cytoplasm: everything inside the plasma membrane except the nucleus: the cytosol plus the organelles.
Organelle: a membrane-bound compartment inside a eukaryotic cell with its own job, such as the ER or a mitochondrion.
Lumen: the space inside a membrane-bound organelle, on the other side of its membrane from the cytosol.
Topology (membrane): which side of a membrane a space or a part of a protein lies on; the lumen of the ER, Golgi, vesicles and lysosomes is topologically equivalent to the outside of the cell.
Nuclear envelope: the two membranes around the nucleus, crossed by nuclear pores; the outer membrane continues into the ER.
Nuclear pore: a large protein channel in the nuclear envelope that joins the nucleoplasm to the cytosol.
Endoplasmic reticulum (ER): a network of membrane sheets and tubes that makes membrane and secreted proteins (rough ER) and lipids (smooth ER), and stores Ca²⁺.
Golgi apparatus: a stack of flattened membrane compartments that modifies proteins from the ER, for example by adding sugar chains, and sorts them to their destinations.
Lysosome: an acidic organelle (pH about 5) full of digestive enzymes that breaks down material taken up by the cell or from the cell itself.
Model system: a simpler organism or cell type (yeast, a cell line, an organoid) chosen because it answers a question more easily than a human body can.
Informed consent: a person’s voluntary agreement, after being told the purpose and risks, to let their tissue or data be used in research.
Cell fractionation: breaking cells open and separating their parts, usually by centrifugation, to find out what each part does.


Seeing cells: microscopy
See Seeing cells: microscopy.
Resolution: the smallest distance at which two points can still be seen as two separate points.
Magnification: how much larger the image is than the object; it adds no detail beyond the resolution limit.
Numerical aperture, NA: how wide a cone of light an objective collects; a higher NA gives better resolution.
Phase-contrast microscopy: turns small delays of light in dense cell parts into differences in brightness, so living unstained cells become visible.
Differential interference contrast, DIC: shows steep changes in optical path as light and shadow, so cells look three-dimensional.
Fluorophore: a molecule that absorbs light of one wavelength and emits light of a longer wavelength.
Stokes shift: the difference in wavelength between a fluorophore’s excitation peak and emission peak.
Dichroic mirror: a mirror that reflects light below a certain wavelength and lets longer wavelengths pass; it separates excitation light from emitted light.
Immunofluorescence: labelling a protein in fixed, permeabilised cells with antibodies coupled, directly or through a secondary antibody, to a fluorophore.
Green fluorescent protein, GFP: a jellyfish protein that forms its own fluorescent group, used as a genetic tag to see proteins in living cells.
Fusion protein: one protein chain made from two genes joined in the same reading frame, for example a protein of interest joined to GFP.
Confocal microscopy: fluorescence microscopy in which a pinhole blocks out-of-focus light, giving a sharp optical section of a thick sample.
Photobleaching: the permanent loss of fluorescence when a fluorophore is destroyed by repeated excitation.
Super-resolution microscopy: light-microscopy methods, such as STED and PALM/STORM, that resolve details below the ~200 nm limit.
Transmission electron microscopy, TEM: electrons pass through an ultrathin, heavy-metal-stained section, showing structures inside the cell at about 1–2 nm.
Scanning electron microscopy, SEM: images the 3D surface of a metal-coated sample by scanning it with a fine electron beam.
Cryo-electron microscopy, cryo-EM: electron microscopy of rapidly frozen samples in glass-like ice; averaging many images of one protein gives its 3D structure.


Taking cells apart and perturbing them
Cell line: a population of cells that has been made immortal and can be grown in culture without limit.
Primary cells: cells taken directly from a tissue, which divide only a limited number of times in culture.
Organoid: a small 3D structure grown from stem cells that contains several cell types of an organ, arranged roughly as in the tissue.
Mycoplasma: very small bacteria without a cell wall that often contaminate cell cultures unnoticed and change how the cells behave.
Differential centrifugation: separating cell components by spinning at increasing speeds, so larger and denser particles form a pellet first.
Density-gradient centrifugation: separating particles by spinning them through a solution that gets denser towards the bottom, so each stops at its own density.
Marker protein: a protein known to be found in only one organelle, used to identify that organelle in a fraction.
Epitope: the small part of a target molecule that an antibody binds.
Western blot: separates proteins by size, transfers them to a membrane and detects one protein with antibodies.
Immunoprecipitation: using an antibody on beads to pull a protein, and the proteins bound to it, out of a cell lysate.
Flow cytometry: measuring light scatter and fluorescence of single cells as they pass a laser one at a time.
Gating: choosing a region in a flow cytometry plot so that only one population of cells is analysed further.
RNA interference, RNAi: lowering the amount of a protein with a short double-stranded RNA that leads to the matching mRNA being cut.
Knockout: disabling a gene completely, for example by a CRISPR-Cas9 cut that causes a frameshift.
